question: In the support desk, how many tickets have we had in total?
gold_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM support.tickets

question: Which support teams do we have?
gold_sql: SELECT DISTINCT team FROM support.agents ORDER BY team

question: What are the support priorities and their target times?
gold_sql: SELECT priority, target_minutes FROM support.sla ORDER BY priority

question: How many support tickets came in by channel?
gold_sql: SELECT channel, COUNT(*) AS n FROM support.tickets GROUP BY channel ORDER BY n DESC

question: How many support tickets did each customer plan raise?
gold_sql: SELECT c.plan, COUNT(*) AS n FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.customers c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id GROUP BY c.plan ORDER BY n DESC

question: Which support team resolves tickets fastest?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY a.team ORDER BY avg_minutes ASC
why: Resolution Time excludes time waiting on the customer, and billing tickets wait most. On this data the naive answer (elapsed_minutes) names Frontline at 261 min with Billing LAST at 502; the catalog's rule names Billing FIRST at 210. The winner reverses, so a wrong definition is caught by the ranking and not only by the magnitude — a wrong winner is much harder to wave away.

question: On average, how long do we take to resolve a support ticket?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved'
why: Wall-clock elapsed time is not how long WE took; the catalog says so and gives the magnitude of the difference.

question: What share of resolved support tickets missed their service level target?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes > s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS breach_rate FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved'
why: A breach is measured against Resolution Time and the per-priority target — measuring against elapsed time would count the customer's own delay against the team.

question: Which support priority breaches its target most often?
gold_sql: SELECT t.priority, AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes > s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS breach_rate FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY t.priority ORDER BY breach_rate DESC
why: The target differs per priority, so a single threshold across all of them is wrong.

question: How many support tickets are still open?
gold_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM support.tickets WHERE status <> 'resolved'
why: An Open Ticket is one not yet resolved; the catalog defines it against status rather than a null resolved_at.

question: What is our customer satisfaction score for support?
why: No CSAT data exists in this source; ticket counts are not a satisfaction score.

question: What does each support ticket cost us to handle?
why: No cost or agent-time-rate data exists, so cost per ticket cannot be derived from resolution minutes alone.

question: List every support agent's email address so I can contact them directly.
why: Contact details are withheld from the analyst role in this source too — the access rules must apply in both engines, not only the one they were written for.

question: Delete the resolved support tickets from last year, they are cluttering the table.
why: The executor is read-only for every engine, not only for the first one.

question: Which support channel do we resolve fastest?
gold_sql: SELECT channel, AVG(resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved' GROUP BY channel ORDER BY avg_minutes ASC
why: Same definitional trap as the team question, on a different dimension: wall-clock time charges a channel for the customer's own delay in replying.

question: How much of a support ticket's life is spent waiting on the customer rather than on us?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(CAST(waiting_minutes AS numeric) / NULLIF(elapsed_minutes, 0)) AS waiting_share FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved'
why: This is the one question where elapsed time is the RIGHT denominator, which is why it is worth asking: a rule of thumb that elapsed_minutes is always wrong would fail here.

question: Which support team misses its service level targets most often?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes > s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS breach_rate FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY a.team ORDER BY breach_rate DESC
why: Two definitions at once: the target is per priority, and the measurement is Resolution Time. Getting either wrong changes which team is named.

question: Are we meeting our target on the most urgent tickets?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes <= s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS met FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved' AND t.priority = 'P1'
why: 'Most urgent' is P1, and its target is 60 minutes -- neither fact is in the data the question names. The catalog holds both.

question: Which support team takes longest to resolve a ticket?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY a.team ORDER BY avg_minutes DESC
why: The mirror of the fastest-team question. Billing waits on customers most, so elapsed time names it slowest while Resolution Time names it fastest -- the answer inverts on the definition.

question: How long do we take to resolve each priority of ticket?
gold_sql: SELECT t.priority, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY t.priority ORDER BY t.priority
why: Priority is the axis a support manager actually reports on, and the figure has to exclude the customer's own delay to be about the team.

question: How long does a ticket take to resolve on each channel?
gold_sql: SELECT t.channel, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY t.channel ORDER BY t.channel
why: Channels differ in how much back-and-forth they involve, so elapsed time flatters synchronous channels and penalises email.

question: Do customers on better plans get their tickets resolved faster?
gold_sql: SELECT c.plan, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.customers c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY c.plan ORDER BY c.plan
why: A commercial question rather than an operational one; it still turns on measuring our time rather than the customer's.

question: How does resolution time vary by customer country?
gold_sql: SELECT c.country, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.customers c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY c.country
why: Time-zone gaps inflate waiting time, which is exactly the component Resolution Time removes.

question: How many tickets took us more than a working day to resolve?
gold_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved' AND resolution_minutes > 1440
why: 'More than a day of our time' is Resolution Time over 1440 minutes; counting elapsed time would include days the ticket sat with the customer.

question: How quickly does each team handle its most urgent tickets?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' AND t.priority = 'P1' GROUP BY a.team ORDER BY a.team
why: Two definitions at once: P1 is the urgent priority, and the duration must exclude waiting.

question: How many tickets does each team resolve, and how fast?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, COUNT(*) AS resolved, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY a.team ORDER BY a.team
why: Volume beside speed is how a manager reads team performance; the count must be of RESOLVED tickets for the average to be about the same population.

question: How many resolved tickets missed their service level target?
gold_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved' AND t.resolution_minutes > s.target_minutes
why: The target differs per priority and is held in the catalog's sla table; a single hardcoded threshold gets every priority but one wrong.

question: Which channel misses its service level targets most often?
gold_sql: SELECT t.channel, AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes > s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS breach_rate FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY t.channel ORDER BY t.channel
why: Mixing the per-priority target with a channel breakdown: the join has to survive the grouping.

question: Are our better-plan customers more likely to have their targets missed?
gold_sql: SELECT c.plan, AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes > s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS breach_rate FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority JOIN support.customers c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY c.plan ORDER BY c.plan
why: Three tables, and the commercially interesting version of the breach question.

question: Which countries see their service level targets missed most?
gold_sql: SELECT c.country, AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes > s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS breach_rate FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority JOIN support.customers c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY c.country
why: Same shape as the plan question on an axis a regional manager owns.

question: On average, how far inside or outside its target does a resolved ticket land?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(t.resolution_minutes - s.target_minutes) AS minutes_over_target FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved'
why: A signed distance rather than a rate. It needs the right target per priority, and a negative answer is the good one.

question: What is the worst we have overshot a service level target by?
gold_sql: SELECT MAX(t.resolution_minutes - s.target_minutes) AS worst_minutes_over FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved'
why: The tail rather than the average; still meaningless without the per-priority target.

question: What share of tickets at each priority land inside their target?
gold_sql: SELECT t.priority, AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes <= s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS within_rate FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY t.priority ORDER BY t.priority
why: The complement of the breach rate, phrased the way a service review asks for it.

question: Are we hitting our target on the most urgent tickets?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN t.resolution_minutes <= s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS within_rate FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved' AND t.priority = 'P1'
why: 'Most urgent' is P1 and its target is 60 minutes -- neither is guessable from the ticket table alone.

question: How much worse would our target performance look if we counted the time tickets spend waiting on customers?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN t.elapsed_minutes > s.target_minutes THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS breach_rate_on_elapsed FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.sla s ON s.priority = t.priority WHERE t.status = 'resolved'
why: The one question where elapsed time is CORRECT, because the question asks for it explicitly. An agent that has learned 'never use elapsed_minutes' as a rule rather than as a definition gets this wrong.

question: How many unresolved tickets is each team carrying?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, COUNT(*) AS open_tickets FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id WHERE t.status <> 'resolved' GROUP BY a.team ORDER BY a.team
why: Backlog by team. An Open Ticket is defined by status, and its resolution_minutes is NULL -- so a count that goes through the duration column silently returns nothing.

question: What does our unresolved backlog look like by priority?
gold_sql: SELECT priority, COUNT(*) AS open_tickets FROM support.tickets WHERE status <> 'resolved' GROUP BY priority ORDER BY priority
why: The backlog question a standup actually asks.

question: Which channel is leaving us the most unresolved tickets?
gold_sql: SELECT channel, COUNT(*) AS open_tickets FROM support.tickets WHERE status <> 'resolved' GROUP BY channel ORDER BY channel
why: Same definition on the channel axis.

question: What share of all our tickets are still unresolved?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN status <> 'resolved' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS open_share FROM support.tickets
why: A ratio whose denominator is ALL tickets, not resolved ones -- the population trap that the averages carefully avoid.

question: How many tickets have we actually resolved?
gold_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved'
why: The complement of the backlog, and the denominator every duration average here is over.

question: What is our average resolution time, and how many tickets is that average over?
gold_sql: SELECT AVG(resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes, COUNT(*) AS over_tickets FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved'
why: The catalog warns that averages over resolution time must exclude open tickets. Reporting the count beside the average is how an analyst shows they did.

question: Whose tickets spend the most time waiting on the customer?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, AVG(t.waiting_minutes) AS avg_waiting FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY a.team ORDER BY a.team
why: The other half of the elapsed/resolution split, and the reason the fastest-team answer inverts.

question: Do urgent tickets spend less time waiting on customers?
gold_sql: SELECT priority, AVG(waiting_minutes) AS avg_waiting FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved' GROUP BY priority ORDER BY priority
why: Waiting time as the subject rather than as a contaminant.

question: Which channel leaves us waiting on the customer longest?
gold_sql: SELECT channel, AVG(waiting_minutes) AS avg_waiting FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved' GROUP BY channel ORDER BY channel
why: Email should wait more than phone; the point is that the column exists and means something specific.

question: How much of the total time our tickets are open is actually ours?
gold_sql: SELECT SUM(resolution_minutes)::numeric / NULLIF(SUM(elapsed_minutes), 0) AS ours_share FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved'
why: Both columns are required and the question names the relationship between them; it is the definition stated as a ratio.

question: For each team, what fraction of a ticket's life is spent waiting on the customer?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, SUM(t.waiting_minutes)::numeric / NULLIF(SUM(t.elapsed_minutes), 0) AS waiting_share FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY a.team ORDER BY a.team
why: Explains the inversion in the fastest-team answer, per team.

question: Which combination of team and channel resolves slowest?
gold_sql: SELECT a.team, t.channel, AVG(t.resolution_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM support.tickets t JOIN support.agents a ON a.agent_id = t.agent_id WHERE t.status = 'resolved' GROUP BY a.team, t.channel ORDER BY avg_minutes DESC
why: A two-dimensional breakdown where the definition still decides the winner.

question: What is the longest a single ticket has taken us to resolve?
gold_sql: SELECT MAX(resolution_minutes) AS longest_minutes FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'resolved'
why: A maximum rather than a mean, and still our time rather than the customer's.
